paragraphs.text: This oolong comes from [Alishan](alishan:where-it-is), the mountain tea area of Chiayi County in the southwest of central Taiwan. Its gardens sit on the western and southern slopes, mostly at about 1,000 to 1,600 metres, and they spread across [three townships](alishan:sub-areas): lower and middle ground in Meishan to the north, Zhuqi with Shizhuo and Fenqihu at the centre, and the higher gardens of Alishan Township along the mountain road. Cloud and fog cover the slopes for much of the day, the sun comes through filtered and the nights are cool, so the leaf grows slowly. The [name on a label](alishan:on-a-label) marks the mountain area as a whole, not one township, garden or height.

It belongs to [high mountain tea](taiwan-oolong:high-mountain), gao shan cha, a name for where a tea grew rather than a cultivar or a recipe: gardens at about 1,000 metres and higher. This one is rolled, the usual form of the style, which is most often lightly oxidised and left unroasted or only lightly roasted. It is a [partly oxidised](oolong:definition) tea, and the plants and the craft of making it reached [Taiwan](taiwan-oolong:definition) with settlers from Fujian.

brewing.text: Ball-rolled Taiwan oolong takes hot water, about 90 to 100°C, a fairly generous amount of leaf and short steeps; the balls open slowly and give many infusions. Roasted Dong Ding takes water from about 95°C to a full boil. Aged oolong takes very hot water, in a pot that holds its heat, clay above all. Oriental Beauty is the exception and takes cooler water, about 80 to 95°C.

notice.text: In light high mountain tea: a sweet, floral cup, often creamy or buttery, with little bitterness and a long sweet aftertaste. In roasted Dong Ding: caramel, ripe fruit, nuts and a toasted aroma. In Baozhong: floral notes and a clear, bright liquor. In Oriental Beauty: ripe fruit and honey, with little bitterness.
